questions.q: How does the summary frame aging?
a: As a loss of information in DNA that can be treated like a disease
As a fixed schedule written permanently into our genes
As mainly a mental attitude toward the passing years
As an unavoidable result of poor childhood nutrition
questions.why: The book treats aging as a disease, and the first lesson explains it as information being lost from our DNA.

questions.q: What do the Blue Zones have in common?
a: Plant-based diets, fasting and a beneficial stress state
High protein intake and daily intense exercise
Constant grazing to avoid ever feeling hungry
Heavy reliance on modern medicine and supplements
questions.why: The second lesson lists a plant-based diet low in animal protein, a fasting period and a desirable state of stress.

questions.q: What are senescent cells, as the summary describes them?
a: Cells that stopped replicating but linger and speed aging
Cells that divide much faster than healthy ones
Cells that repair damaged DNA in other tissues
Cells that carry oxygen through the bloodstream
questions.why: The third lesson calls them zombie cells: they forgot how to replicate, are not dead, and affect the healthy cells around them.

a: Nutrients that help the body get rid of zombie cells
Drugs that lengthen the protective caps on DNA
Exercises that deliberately stress the body
Genes that permanently block cell division
questions.why: The summary names senolytics as nutrients found in kale, red onion and capers that help clear senescent cells.

a: Reprogramming cells from a seed that has stayed intact
Freezing healthy cells for use later in life
Editing genes to remove inherited mutations
Transplanting organs from younger donors
questions.why: The third lesson calls it reprogramming cells from the seed that has remained unchanged since conception.
